speaker: Patient
text: 65-year-old female. The patient is here for an annual well-check. She has a history of well-controlled diabetes and hypertension, managed with metformin and losartan, respectively. She reports maintaining a healthy diet primarily consisting of vegetables and lean meat, denies any tobacco or alcohol use, and enjoys outdoor activities like walking and sunbathing.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for the detailed history; given your age and outdoor habits, could you describe the appearance of the lesion—specifically its color, texture, and whether it has been growing or bleeding? Also, have you noticed any changes in sensation or pain in this area?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is The presence of a rough, scaly, sandpaper-like plaque on the left dorsal hand. I also have No tenderness, No pain.

speaker: Doctor
text:
That description of a rough, sandpaper-like plaque is very characteristic of a sun-induced change. Given your history of sunbathing, are you sure the lesion has not changed in size or color over the past few years?

REQUEST TEST: Dermoscopy of left dorsal hand lesion.
REQUEST IMAGES: Clinical_photo_left_hand.

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: Diabetes, Hypertension Social history: Non-smoker, denies alcohol use, enjoys outdoor activities

speaker: Patient
text: Unremarkable except for the skin condition described. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Urinary tract infection and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text:
That is certainly an unusual comment; a UTI does not present as a rough, scaly plaque on the hand. Looking at the clinical photo and dermoscopy, do you see any ulceration, atypical pigment network, or distinct vascular patterns that might suggest a different etiology?

Also, could you clarify if this specific area ever resolves spontaneously or if it requires treatment to fade?

DIAGNOSIS READY: Actinic Keratosis
